svg.title: Selection criteria for trimodality therapy: the EAU, AUA and NICE wordings side by side, with the NICE column empty
svg.desc: Schematic setting the three guidelines' wording on who is suitable for trimodality therapy side by side as one table: three columns for EAU 2026, AUA/ASCO/SUO 2024 and NICE NG2, and six rows for number of tumours and stage, carcinoma in situ, hydronephrosis, resection, bladder function and histological subtype. The figure first states the shape of the evidence: comparing trimodality therapy with radical cystectomy there is no successfully completed randomised trial, the trial that closed for insufficient accrual was SPARE with only 45 patients, and so the criteria in the table are guideline wording rather than thresholds calculated from a randomised trial. The EAU column quotes verbatim: for number and stage "solitary, unifocal cT2-T3a tumours"; for carcinoma in situ "absence of extensive or multifocal CIS"; for hydronephrosis "no or unilateral hydronephrosis"; for resection, that as much visible tumour as possible should be resected and that on a second resection more than half of cases turn out to have residual disease; for bladder function "good baseline bladder function"; and for histological subtype that urothelial carcinoma with squamous, glandular or micropapillary differentiation may be considered while pure squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma should be advised surgery instead. The same EAU paragraph adds that patient selection is the key to good outcomes. The AUA column quotes verbatim: "Patients with large tumors unable to be resected by TURBT, multifocal CIS, T3/T4 tumors, and/or hydronephrosis are not ideal candidates for any type of bladder preserving therapy."; the ideal candidate for carcinoma in situ is written as "no CIS" with random biopsies advised to confirm it; hydronephrosis is written as "no hydronephrosis" with no sentence allowing a unilateral one; resection is written as "complete resection is feasible", with statement 22 asking for a maximal debulking resection; and on histological subtype, adenocarcinoma, sarcoma and squamous cell carcinoma were not included in any prospective radiation-based bladder preservation study. The AUA bladder-function cell is drawn as a dash, with a note that a dash means this figure did not take a corresponding wording from that document, not that the guideline has no view on the item. The whole NICE NG2 column is drawn empty with a hatched fill and labelled: this column is empty, NICE NG2 gives no tumour criteria at all, and nothing was left out or is still being looked up. Below the table a separate box records that what NICE gives is a process rather than tumour criteria: 1.5.5 "Offer a choice of radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser"; 1.5.6 requires a urological surgeon who performs radical cystectomy, a clinical oncologist and a clinical nurse specialist to be part of the discussion; and 1.5.7 requires the discussion to cover that the limited evidence cannot establish whether surgery or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser gives the better outcome, along with the effects of each on sexual and bowel function and the risk of death from the treatment itself. Below that, only three things are common to all three documents: a multidisciplinary team, shared decision-making, and that radiotherapy alone is not an option, the AUA statement reading "clinicians should not offer radiation therapy alone as a curative treatment". The figure closes with two readings it must not be given - "anyone who would rather not have surgery can have this" and "I can check myself against this" - stating that this is not a tick-box list, that beyond the tumour criteria there is whether the kidneys can carry the chemotherapy, bladder function and whether the resection can be complete, none of which can be read off without the reports and a cystoscopy, and that the three guidelines are worded differently and that is not a slip, so take your own tumour details and ask which clauses of which guideline you meet.

g.text: TRIMODALITY THERAPY - WHO IS A CANDIDATE, IN THREE GUIDELINES' OWN WORDS
Who is a candidate for trimodality therapy: three
guidelines, three wordings, and one that gives no criteria
at all
This figure sets the three guidelines' own wording on who is suitable for trimodality therapy side by side. The wordings differ, and that is
neither a slip nor a translation problem - the three documents are simply written differently.
This is not a tick-box eligibility list. The criteria interact, and the same criterion has a different threshold in different guidelines; whether
you meet them is for a multidisciplinary team to judge.
First, the shape of the evidence: comparing trimodality therapy with radical cystectomy, there is no successfully completed randomised trial (the trial that
closed for insufficient accrual was SPARE, with only 45 patients). So the criteria below are guideline wording, not thresholds calculated from a randomised
trial.
EAU 2026
AUA/ASCO/SUO 2024
NICE NG2
Number of tumours
and stage
"solitary, unifocal cT2-T3a tumours".
"Patients with large tumors unable to be
resected by TURBT, multifocal CIS, T3/T4
tumors, and/or hydronephrosis are not ideal
candidates for any type of bladder
preserving therapy."
Carcinoma in situ
"absence of extensive or multifocal CIS".
The ideal candidate is written as "no CIS",
with random biopsies advised to confirm it.
Hydronephrosis
"no or unilateral hydronephrosis".
The ideal candidate is written as "no
hydronephrosis"; the AUA has no sentence
allowing a unilateral one.
Resection
When trimodality therapy is planned, as much
visible tumour as possible should be
resected; and on a second resection, more
than half of cases turn out to have residual
disease.
The ideal candidate is written as "complete
resection is feasible"; statement 22 asks for
a maximal debulking resection in anyone
considering bladder preservation, with
assessment for multifocal disease and
carcinoma in situ.
Bladder function
"good baseline bladder function".
Histological subtype
Urothelial carcinoma with squamous,
glandular or micropapillary differentiation
has complete response, survival and salvage
cystectomy rates close to pure urothelial
carcinoma and may be considered; but pure
squamous cell carcinoma or
adenocarcinoma does worse after
trimodality therapy, and surgery should be
advised instead.
Adenocarcinoma, sarcoma and squamous
cell carcinoma were not included in any
prospective radiation-based bladder
preservation study, and should not be treated
this way unless the patient is unfit for
surgery.
This column is empty
NICE NG2 gives no tumour criteria at all.
This cell is empty - nothing was left out,
and nothing is still being looked up.
"-" means this figure did not take a corresponding wording from that document. It does not mean that guideline has no view on the item.
In the same paragraph the EAU adds one sentence: patient selection is the key to good outcomes.
What NICE gives is a process, not tumour criteria
1.5.5: "Offer a choice of radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser".
1.5.6: the discussion must include a urological surgeon who performs radical cystectomy, a clinical oncologist and a clinical nurse specialist.
1.5.7: the discussion must cover that the limited evidence cannot establish whether surgery or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser gives the better outcome, along
with the effects of each on sexual and bowel function and the risk of death from the treatment itself.
Only three things are common to all three documents
a multidisciplinary team
the team decides, not one specialty on its own
shared decision-making
both roads are discussed before anything is
decided
radiotherapy alone is not an option
the AUA statement reads "clinicians should not
offer radiation therapy alone as a curative
treatment"
Two readings this figure must not be given
"anyone who would rather not have surgery can have this"
The criteria are set out item by item, and the three guidelines word them
differently; whether you meet them is for a multidisciplinary team to judge.
"I can check myself against this"
This is not a tick-box list. Beyond the tumour criteria there is whether the
kidneys can carry the chemotherapy, bladder function, and whether the
resection can be complete - none of which can be read off without the reports
and a cystoscopy.
The three guidelines are worded differently, and that is not a slip. Take your own tumour details and ask: which clauses of which guideline do I meet?
Schematic, redrawn from the EAU guidelines on muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (2026 edition), the AUA/ASCO/SUO 2024 guideline, NICE NG2 and SPARE
(Huddart 2017); not reproduced from their figures. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
